name: Anti-Corruption Layer
intent: Put a translating layer between a new system and a legacy one, so the legacy model and its quirks never leak into the new design.
scenario: A new billing service must read customers from an old CRM. The CRM returns names as LOVELACE, ADA, one-letter status codes and balances as zero-padded cents.
problem: Billing reads the CRM's fields directly. Status codes, name formats and padded numbers spread through its code, so billing now thinks in the CRM's terms. Every CRM quirk becomes a billing bug, and the old system's design shapes the new one.
solution: A layer between the two translates in both directions. It calls the CRM, turns each record into a clean Customer in billing's own language (a full name, an active or closed status, a balance in cents) and rejects what it cannot understand. Billing talks only to the layer. Where one system's model ends and the other's begins is one visible, tested place. This goes further than an Adapter, which only changes an interface: the layer also translates meaning and protects the design on the new side.
pain: Billing code is full of CRM field names and status codes
Billing's model has been bent to match the CRM's
A change in the CRM breaks several places in billing
New developers must learn the CRM's quirks to work on billing
benefits: Billing keeps a clean model in its own language
CRM quirks are handled in one tested place
A change in the CRM changes only the layer
When the CRM is replaced, the layer is replaced and billing is untouched
whenToUse: A new system must work with a legacy or third-party system whose model you do not want to adopt
You are migrating step by step, as in the strangler fig approach, and old and new live side by side
The two sides use different meanings for the same words
whenNotToUse: The other system's model is already good and close to yours: a thin adapter is enough
A throw-away script that will be deleted soon
When the two models are the same on purpose, as in a conformist relationship
pitfalls: The legacy terms slowly creep back into the new code because it is quicker, and the layer stops protecting anything
The layer grows business rules and becomes a second application
Translation hides data the legacy system gives you, so a field that matters is silently dropped
It is one more thing to run and keep in sync, and it can become a bottleneck or a single point of failure

roles.label: New system
roles.description: Billing. It has a clean model and uses only its own words.

roles.label: Anti-corruption layer
roles.description: Translates between the two models: a gateway that fetches, and a translator that converts and rejects.

roles.label: Legacy system
roles.description: The CRM, with its own model, codes and formats that must not leak.

quiz.question: A new billing service reads the legacy CRM directly. Its code has checks such as status == "A" and names split on a comma in many files. What is the best change?
options: Add comments next to each check that explain what the CRM's codes mean
Place a layer between them that turns CRM records into billing's own clean Customer objects
Ask the CRM team to change its codes so that they match billing's naming
Copy the CRM's table into the billing database, and read the copy instead of the CRM
quiz.explanation: The legacy model is spreading through billing's code. An anti-corruption layer translates once at the boundary, so billing only sees its own model. Comments keep the codes, the CRM may not change, and a copy of the table has the same shape and the same problem.

quiz.question: Six months after adding an anti-corruption layer, developers start returning the CRM's raw status code inside billing's Customer object because it is quicker than adding a new status. What is the likely result?
options: Billing becomes faster, since the layer does less work to translate each customer
Nothing changes, because the layer still exists and still sits between the two systems
The CRM team can now change its codes without any warning, because billing is independent
The legacy model leaks back in, and the layer protects less and less of the new design
quiz.explanation: The point of the layer is that billing never sees the CRM's terms. Once raw codes cross it, billing code depends on them again, and a CRM change breaks billing. Keep the layer's output free of legacy terms, and test the translation.

quiz.question: In two years the legacy CRM will be replaced with a modern customer service. What does the anti-corruption layer give the billing team at that point?
options: A single place to replace: a new gateway for the new service, and billing code that stays unchanged
Nothing, since the layer is thrown away and every billing file is rewritten for the new service
A copy of the CRM's old data, which can be searched if the new service has gaps
A guarantee that the new service will use the same codes and formats as the old one did
quiz.explanation: Because billing only knows its own model, swapping the CRM means writing a new translation behind the same interface. Without the layer, the old CRM's terms are all over billing and every file would change. The layer holds no data and guarantees nothing about the new service.
